paragraphs.heading: The worst extinction known
paragraphs.text: The Permian–Triassic extinction happened around the boundary between the Permian and Triassic periods, which is also the line between the Paleozoic and Mesozoic eras. It is the most severe extinction event known on Earth and the greatest of the "Big Five" of the Phanerozoic. It wiped out 57% of biological families and 62% of genera. Among species, 81% of marine ones and 70% of land vertebrates were lost. It is also the largest known mass extinction of insects.

paragraphs.heading: Volcanoes and carbon
paragraphs.text: Scientists broadly agree that the main cause was the flood basalt eruptions that built the Siberian Traps. These released sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide, which raised global temperatures, acidified the oceans and caused euxinia, a state of oxygen-starved, sulfurous seas. Carbon dioxide in the air climbed from around 400 ppm to 2,500 ppm, as some 3,900 to 12,000 gigatonnes of carbon entered the oceans and atmosphere. For comparison, the level just before the Industrial Revolution was 280 ppm, and today it is about 426 ppm.

paragraphs.heading: Dating the disaster
paragraphs.text: Rock sequences across the boundary were once thought too few and too patchy to study in detail, but the extinction can now be dated to within thousands of years. Five volcanic ash beds at Meishan in China, the official reference section for the boundary, give a high-resolution timeline. The boundary itself is marked by the first appearance of a conodont called Hindeodus parvus. Its start is dated to 251.941 ± 0.037 million years ago and its end to 251.880 ± 0.031 million years ago, a span of 60 ± 48 thousand years.

paragraphs.heading: Chemical fingerprints
paragraphs.text: The extinction lines up with a large, sudden worldwide drop in δ¹³C, the ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12. That drop helps locate the boundary in rocks that cannot be dated by radiometric methods. There is also evidence that more ultraviolet radiation reached Earth, causing mutations in plant spores. Some researchers have tied the boundary to a "fungal spike", a surge in fungi feeding on the mass of dead plants and animals. Critics suggest the most common supposed fungal spore may be a fossil alga, but newer chemical evidence fits a fungal origin better.

paragraphs.heading: Fast or slow
paragraphs.text: How long the whole extinction took is still uncertain. Some evidence points to several pulses, or to a long decline stretched across a few million years that peaked sharply in the final million years of the Permian. Different groups seem to have died out at different times; the losses of ostracods and of brachiopods, for example, came roughly 670,000 to 1.17 million years apart. The picture is muddied by the earlier Capitanian extinction, and many losses once placed at the Permian–Triassic boundary have since been re-dated to the end of the Capitanian.

paragraphs.heading: Land and sea
paragraphs.text: Another open question is whether life on land and in the sea collapsed at the same time. A well-preserved sequence in east Greenland suggests both began together, with animal life declining over about 10,000 to 60,000 years. In that same sequence, plants took several hundred thousand years more to show the full impact. Other scientists think the land extinction began 60,000 to 370,000 years before the marine one, and dating in the Karoo Basin also places the land losses earlier.
